35110.e: Newspapers, radio, television and the internet report on the proposals. There are also discussion programmes.
35110.m: You can find out about votes in newspapers and programmes.

35111.q: In a Swiss vote, what is a party's “Parole”?
a: A recommendation for Yes or No
35111.e: Parties and associations issue a “Parole”. With it they recommend Yes or No to their members.
35111.m: A “Parole” is a recommendation for Yes or No.

35112.q: Why should you find out about the issues before a vote?
a: So that you can decide well
So that you fall asleep faster
So that you do not have to vote
35112.e: If you know what it is about, you can decide better. That is why it is worth listening to both sides.
35112.m: If you find out about the issues, you can decide better.

35113.q: Besides the printed booklet, where else does the Confederation provide voting information?
a: On the internet and in an app
35113.e: The voting information is also available on the internet. The Confederation even offers its own app for it.
35113.m: You can also find voting information on the internet.

35114.q: In which languages, among others, is the federal voting booklet available?
35114.e: Switzerland has several national languages. That is why the booklet is available in German, French and Italian, and partly also in Romansh.
35114.m: The voting booklet is available in the national languages.

a: More Yes than No votes in the whole country
35115.e: For the popular majority, all the votes in the whole of Switzerland are added together. If there are more Yes than No votes, the popular majority is reached.
35115.m: The popular majority is reached when there are more Yes than No votes in the whole of Switzerland.

35116.q: How much is each single vote worth for the popular majority?
35116.e: For the popular majority every vote counts exactly the same. It does not matter where someone lives.
35116.m: For the popular majority every vote counts the same.

35117.q: 1000 people vote Yes or No. What is the smallest number of Yes votes needed for a majority?
35117.e: Half of 1000 is 500. A majority needs more than half, so at least 501 votes.
35117.m: A majority needs more than half of the votes.

35118.q: Of 800 valid votes, 300 are Yes. How many are No?
35118.e: You calculate 800 minus 300 = 500. So there are 500 No votes, and No has the majority.
35118.m: You find the No votes by taking the Yes votes away from the total.

35119.q: Who makes up “the people” in a vote?
35119.e: “The people” means everyone who has voted. Their votes together make up the popular majority.
35119.m: For the popular majority, the votes of everyone who votes count.

35120.q: With 600 Yes and 400 No: how many more votes does Yes have?
35120.e: You calculate 600 minus 400 = 200. So Yes has 200 more votes.
35120.m: You find the lead by taking the smaller number away from the bigger one.

35121.q: Do blank ballot papers count as Yes for the popular majority?
35121.e: Blank ballot papers are counted neither as Yes nor as No. For the popular majority, only the Yes and No votes are compared.
35121.m: Blank ballot papers do not count as Yes for the popular majority.

35122.q: A proposal gets 52 per cent Yes. What percentage is No?
35122.e: Yes and No together make 100 per cent. You calculate 100 minus 52 = 48.
35122.m: Yes and No together make 100 per cent.

35123.q: What is the majority of the cantons?
a: The majority of cantons voting Yes
35123.e: For the majority of the cantons, what counts is how many cantons said Yes. If there are more Yes cantons than No cantons, it is reached.
35123.m: The majority of the cantons means more cantons say Yes than No.

35124.q: How many whole cantonal votes do most cantons have?
35124.e: Most cantons have exactly one cantonal vote. Only a few cantons have half a vote.
35124.m: Most cantons have one cantonal vote.

35125.q: What is the smallest number of cantonal votes a proposal needs for the majority of the cantons?
35125.e: There are 23 cantonal votes; half of that is 11.5. A majority needs more than half, so at least 12.
35125.m: The majority of the cantons needs at least 12 cantonal votes.

35126.q: When is the majority of the cantons needed as well as the popular majority?
35126.e: For changes to the Federal Constitution, for example popular initiatives, both the people and the cantons are needed. This is called the double majority.
35126.m: Changes to the Constitution need the popular majority and the majority of the cantons.

35127.q: What happens if a popular initiative gets the popular majority but not the majority of the cantons?
a: There is another vote straight away
35127.e: A popular initiative needs both: the popular majority and the majority of the cantons. If one of them is missing, it is rejected.
35127.m: Without the majority of the cantons, a popular initiative is rejected.

35128.q: For the majority of the cantons, you count how many cantons say Yes. How many cantons does Switzerland have?
35128.e: Switzerland has 26 cantons. For the majority of the cantons, you look at whether more cantons say Yes than No.

35129.q: Why is there a majority of the cantons?
a: So that small cantons also carry weight
So that there are more posters
35129.e: Without the majority of the cantons, the large cantons with many inhabitants would decide almost alone. The majority of the cantons protects the small cantons.
35129.m: The majority of the cantons gives small cantons weight too.

35130.q: Which canton counts only half for the majority of the cantons?
35130.e: Six cantons have only half a cantonal vote, for example Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden and Obwalden.
35130.m: Appenzell Ausserrhoden has only half a vote for the majority of the cantons.

35131.q: On a voting Sunday, do you have to vote the same way on all proposals?
a: No, you decide afresh on each one
35131.e: Each proposal deals with a different topic. That is why you decide afresh on each question.
35131.m: You decide afresh on each proposal.

35132.q: What do you call it when someone goes to the polling station to vote?
35132.e: At the polling station you put your ballot paper into the ballot box. That is why people say “going to the polls”.
35132.m: Anyone who votes at the polling station goes to the polls.

35133.q: What does it mean if the Federal Council recommends accepting a proposal?
35133.e: In the voting booklet the Federal Council says what it recommends. But it is the voters who decide.
35133.m: The Federal Council gives a recommendation, but the people decide.

35134.q: What do you do with the ballot paper before putting it in the envelope?
35134.e: First you write Yes or No on the ballot paper. Then you put it in the envelope and send it back.
35134.m: You fill in the ballot paper before putting it in the envelope.

35135.q: From what age can you stand for the National Council?
35135.e: Anyone who is entitled to vote at 18 can be elected to the National Council. There is no higher minimum age.
35135.m: You can stand for the National Council from the age of 18.

35136.q: What is the youth group of a party, which often has its own election lists, called?
35136.e: Many parties have a youth party for young members. In elections, youth parties often stand with their own lists.
35136.m: Youth parties are the youth groups of the parties.

35137.q: What is on the National Council list next to a candidate's name?
35137.e: Besides the name, the election list also shows the year of birth, job and place of residence. That way you know better who is standing.
35137.m: The election list also shows job and place of residence.

35138.q: Are the votes of Swiss citizens abroad also counted in the National Council election?
35138.e: Swiss citizens abroad who have registered may vote. Their votes are counted in their voting canton.
35138.m: The votes of Swiss citizens abroad are counted too.

35140.q: What does a new group need for its list to be accepted for the National Council election?
a: Signatures of people entitled to vote
35140.e: New lists must be signed by a certain number of people entitled to vote. Parties that are already in Parliament usually do not need this.
35140.m: A new list needs signatures of people entitled to vote.

35141.q: What do you call a person who does not belong to any party?
35141.e: Anyone who does not belong to a party is an independent. Independent people may also stand for election.
35141.m: Independents may stand for election too.

35142.q: What do you call a person who is already in office and stands again?
35142.e: People who already hold an office are called incumbents. Anyone standing for the first time is a new candidate.
35142.m: Incumbents already hold the office and want to keep it.

35143.q: What does an election poster often show?
35143.e: On election posters you often see a face, a name and a short slogan. This is so that people remember the person.
35143.m: Election posters show who would like to be elected.

35144.q: What is an election poster for?
a: Showing the way to the station
35144.e: An election poster is advertising. It is meant to get people to vote for a particular person or party.
35144.m: An election poster asks for votes.

35145.q: Apart from the photo, what can you see on many election posters?
35145.e: On election posters you often see the logo and colour of the party. That way you quickly recognise which party someone belongs to.
35145.m: The party logo shows which party someone belongs to.

35146.q: What happens to the election posters after the election?
35146.e: After the election the posters are no longer needed. The parties have to clear them away again.
35146.m: After the election the posters disappear again.

35147.q: May you simply destroy other people's election posters?
35147.e: Election posters belong to someone. Anyone who damages them commits criminal damage and can be punished.
35147.m: You must not damage other people's election posters.

35148.q: What is usually written in big letters on an election poster?
35148.e: So that people know whom they can vote for, the name is written in big letters on the poster. That makes it easy to remember.
35148.m: The name is written in big letters on the election poster.

35149.q: What do you call a short saying on an election poster?
35149.e: A slogan is a short sentence that is easy to remember. It is meant to show the party's idea quickly.
35149.m: A slogan is a short advertising saying.

35150.q: Who decides where election posters may be put up in a municipality?
35150.e: Posters on public land need rules. The municipality decides where and for how long posters may stand.
35150.m: The municipality decides where posters may stand.

35151.q: What is on an election list?
35151.e: An election list shows the names of the people you can vote for. In the National Council election each party has one or more lists.
35151.m: An election list shows the names of the candidates.

35152.q: What is it called when you write the same name twice on the election list?
35152.e: Cumulating means piling up. In this way the person gets more than one vote from one voter.
35152.m: When cumulating, I write a name twice.

35153.q: What is it called when you write names from another party onto your list?
35153.e: Panachage comes from the French word for mixing. You mix names from different lists.
35153.m: With panachage I mix names from different lists.

35154.q: What happens if you put in a pre-printed party list without any changes?
a: You vote for all the people on it
You only vote for the first person
35154.e: Anyone who puts in an unchanged list gives a vote to everyone on the list. The votes also count for the party.
35154.m: An unchanged list gives a vote to everyone on it.

35155.q: What may you do with a name on a pre-printed election list if you do not want that person?
35155.e: You may cross out names you do not want to vote for. You may still put the list in.
35155.m: I may cross out names on the list.

35156.q: How must you make changes on the election paper?
35156.e: Changes on the election paper must be handwritten. That way it is clear that the voter made them personally.
35156.m: I write changes on the election paper by hand.

35157.q: What is an election paper without pre-printed names called?
35157.e: There are no names on the blank list. You write the people you want to vote for yourself.
35157.m: On the blank list I write the names myself.

35158.q: Apart from its name, how do you recognise each list in the National Council election?
35158.e: Each list gets a number and a name. With the list number you can find it again quickly.
35158.m: Every election list has its own number.

35159.q: In which month do the newly elected National Councillors start work after the election?
35159.e: After the election in autumn, the new Parliament meets for the winter session in December. Then the new term of office begins.
35159.m: The newly elected Parliament starts in the winter session in December.

35160.q: What is a term of office?
a: The time someone holds an office
The opening hours of the post office
The length of a school lesson
35160.e: A term of office begins after the election and ends with the next election. During this time the person carries out their task.
35160.m: The term of office is the time someone holds an office.

35162.q: How long is a term of office in the Council of States in most cantons?
35162.e: The cantons decide this themselves. But almost everywhere, members of the Council of States are elected for four years.
35162.m: Members of the Council of States are usually elected for four years too.

35163.q: How long is a term of office of the President of the USA?
35163.e: The President of the USA is elected every four years. The election takes place in November.
35163.m: In the USA the President is elected every four years.

35164.q: How long is the term of office of the President of France?
35164.e: Since 2002 the French President has been elected for five years. Before that it was seven years.
35164.m: In France the President's term of office is five years.

35165.q: What happens at the end of a term of office?
35165.e: When a term of office ends, there is a new election. That way the people regularly have a say in who governs.
35165.m: After every term of office there is a new election.

35166.q: Why do terms of office not last for ever?
a: So that the people can decide again
So that there are fewer laws
35166.e: In a democracy, power is only given for a limited time. At the next election the people can elect other people.
35166.m: In a democracy you only hold an office for a limited time.

35167.q: What does a person get when they are elected to the National Council?
35167.e: Elected people get a seat in the National Council. There they may take part in debates and vote.
35167.m: Anyone who is elected gets a seat in the council.

35168.q: What must an elected person do after the election?
35168.e: An elected person must say whether they want to take up the office. Only then do they take it up.
35168.m: After the election you accept or decline the office.

35169.q: What is an election called where there are as many candidates as seats, so nobody has to vote?
35169.e: If no more people stand than there are seats, they are elected without a vote. This is called a tacit election.
35169.m: In a tacit election no vote is needed.

35170.q: What happens in the National Council when a member steps down?
a: The next person on the list moves up
35170.e: In the National Council, the person who had the most votes on the same list but was not elected moves up. So no new election is needed.
35170.m: When someone steps down, someone from the same list moves up.

35171.q: What do members of the National Council get for their work?
35171.e: Council members get an allowance for sittings and preparation. Many also have another job alongside.
35171.m: National Council members get an allowance for their work.

35172.q: What usually happens in the Council of States election if nobody gets enough votes in the first round?
35172.e: In some elections you need more than half of the votes in the first round. If nobody manages this, there is a second vote.
35172.m: If nobody has enough votes, there is a second round.

35173.q: What is a majority of more than half of all votes called?
35173.e: An absolute majority means more than half of the votes. It is usually needed in the first round of the Council of States election.
35173.m: An absolute majority is more than half of the votes.

35174.q: Whoever has the most votes in the second round is elected. What is this majority called?
35174.e: With a relative majority it is enough to have more votes than everyone else. You do not then need more than half.
35174.m: With a relative majority, whoever has the most votes wins.

a: What someone promises before the election
35175.e: Before the election, candidates say what they want to do. These are called election promises.
35175.m: An election promise says what someone wants to do after the election.

35176.q: When do candidates make election promises?
35176.e: With promises, candidates want to win voters over. That is why they make them before the election.
35176.m: You hear election promises before the election.

35177.q: Can a National Councillor carry out an election promise alone?
35177.e: In Parliament the majority decides. A single person must convince many others for a law to be made.
35177.m: A new law needs a majority.

35178.q: What can voters do if someone does not keep their promises?
35178.e: An election promise is not a contract. But at the next election you can vote for someone else.
35178.m: At the next election I can vote for someone else.

35179.q: What is the booklet in which a party writes down its goals called?
35179.e: The party programme says what a party wants to work for. Many election promises come from it.
35179.m: The party programme contains a party's goals.

35180.q: Which election promise can a municipal councillor really keep?
35180.e: A good promise is achievable. A municipal councillor really can work for a playground.

35181.q: Why should you check election promises carefully?
a: Because not everything can be done
Because they are only for children
35181.e: Some things sound good but are expensive or difficult. That is why it is worth thinking about whether a promise is realistic.
35181.m: I check whether a promise is realistic.

35182.q: What can voters check after four years?
a: What has become of the promises
35182.e: At the end of a term of office you can see what has been achieved. Then you can decide afresh at the election.
35182.m: After four years I can compare what was promised and what was done.

35183.q: How many election papers may a person put in for the National Council election?
35183.e: Every voter may hand in exactly one election paper. But they can change or add names on it.
35183.m: In the National Council election I put in only one election paper.

35184.q: How many names may you write on your election paper in the National Council election?
a: As many as the canton has seats
35184.e: You have as many votes as your canton has seats in the National Council. In cantons with only one seat, you therefore write only one name.
35184.m: My number of votes depends on my canton's seats.

35185.q: In which year will the next National Council elections take place (as of 2026)?
35185.e: The last election was in 2023. Four years later, in 2027, there will be another election.
35185.m: The next National Council elections are in 2027.

35186.q: What forms a constituency in the National Council election?
35186.e: Each canton elects its own National Council members. That is why each canton is a constituency.
35186.m: In the National Council election each canton is a constituency.

35187.q: Roughly how many people stood for the National Council in 2023?
35187.e: In 2023 there were almost 6000 candidates, more than ever before. Only a small number of them could be elected.
35187.m: In 2023 almost 6000 people stood for the National Council.

35188.q: Roughly how many people voted in the 2023 National Council election?
a: Just under half of those entitled to vote
35188.e: Turnout in 2023 was around 47 per cent. That is just under half of those entitled to vote.
35188.m: In 2023 just under half of those entitled to vote voted.

35189.q: In the National Council election, may you write a person on the list who is not standing at all?
35189.e: In the National Council election you can only vote for people who are on an official list. Other names are not counted.
35189.m: In the National Council election only names of candidates count.

35190.q: Which system is used in the National Council election in cantons with several seats?
35190.e: With proportional representation, the lists get as many seats as matches their share of the votes. That way smaller parties are represented too.
35190.m: With proportional representation, parties get seats according to their share of the votes.

35191.q: Roughly what percentage of the National Council members elected in 2023 were women?
35191.e: In 2023, 77 women were elected to the National Council. That is around 39 per cent of the 200 seats.
35191.m: In 2023 nearly 4 in 10 of those elected to the National Council were women.

35192.q: What is the time before an election when people ask for votes called?
35192.e: In the election campaign, parties and candidates try to convince as many people as possible. The word “campaign” here means a peaceful contest.
35192.m: In the election campaign, candidates ask for votes.

35193.q: What do parties often hand out in the street during an election campaign?
35193.e: Leaflets are small sheets of paper with information about the party. They are handed out at stands in markets and squares.
35193.m: In the election campaign, parties hand out leaflets.

35194.q: What is it called when a party talks to people from a small stand at the market?
35194.e: At a street stand, party members stand at a table. They hand out material and talk to passers-by.
35194.m: At a street stand I can talk to candidates.

35195.q: What is an event called where candidates debate with each other in front of an audience?
35195.e: In a panel discussion, several candidates sit at the front. They answer questions and debate with each other.
35195.m: At a panel discussion I compare the candidates' opinions.

35196.q: What is a well-known Swiss website that shows which candidates match your own opinion called?
35196.e: On Smartvote you answer questions on political topics. Then you see which candidates think in a similar way.
35196.m: Smartvote helps you compare the candidates.

35197.q: What should a fair election campaign be like?
35197.e: In an election campaign you may criticise other opinions. But you should stay respectful and tell the truth.
35197.m: A good election campaign is fair and honest.

35198.q: How much does an election campaign with posters and adverts cost?
35198.e: Posters, leaflets and adverts have to be paid for. The money comes from the parties and their supporters.
35198.m: An election campaign costs a lot of money.

35199.q: Where else do many candidates campaign today?
a: In the credits at the cinema
35199.e: Many candidates show themselves on the internet with videos and pictures. That way they also reach young people.
35199.m: Today election campaigns also take place on the internet.

35200.q: What does the computer help with when an election is counted?
35200.e: The votes are recorded and then added up by computer. That way the results come faster.
35200.m: The computer helps to add up the votes.

35201.q: When are the votes counted in the National Council election?
a: On the Monday before the election
35201.e: After the polls close on Sunday, the counting begins. By the evening there are already many results.
35201.m: The votes are counted on election Sunday.

35202.q: Why does counting a National Council election take longer than a vote?
a: Because counting only starts on Monday
35202.e: In a vote you only count Yes and No. In the election many names and lists have to be recorded, which takes more time.
35202.m: Counting an election takes longer than counting a vote.

35203.q: What happens to an election paper with insults written on it?
35203.e: Election papers with offensive remarks are invalid. They are not counted.
35203.m: An election paper with insults does not count.

35204.q: What is money that people give a party voluntarily called?
35204.e: A donation is voluntary. Parties use donations to pay, for example, for posters and adverts.
35204.m: A donation is money given voluntarily.

35205.q: What does a poll before the election show?
a: How the election might turn out
When the posters are put up
35205.e: In a poll, a few thousand people are asked before the election. It shows a mood, but the real result can be different.
35205.m: A poll only shows how the election might turn out.

35206.q: Where can you see the results on election evening?
35206.e: On election Sunday, television, radio and the internet report live. The Confederation and the cantons also publish the results online.
35206.m: On election evening I can see the results on television and the internet.

35207.q: What does the final result of a National Council election show?
a: How many seats each party gets
Who handed out the most leaflets
What the weather was like on election day
35207.e: After counting, it is clear how many seats each party gets and which people are elected.
35207.m: The final result shows each party's seats.

35208.q: Who is the winner of an election?
35208.e: The winner is whoever won the most votes or seats. Parties that gain a lot are often called winners too.
35208.m: The election winner did best in the election.

35209.q: Which party gained the most seats in the National Council in 2023?
35209.e: The SVP gained nine seats in 2023. That was the biggest gain of all the parties.
35209.m: In 2023 the SVP made the biggest gains in the National Council.

35210.q: Which party lost the most seats in the National Council in 2023?
35210.e: The Green Liberals lost six seats in 2023. The Greens lost five seats.
35210.m: In 2023 the Green Liberals lost the most seats in the National Council.

35211.q: Which party had the most seats in the Council of States after the 2023 election?
35211.e: In the Council of States, the Centre had 15 seats after the 2023 election. The FDP and SP came next.
35211.m: In the Council of States, the Centre was the strongest party after the 2023 election.

35212.q: What is it called when a party gets more seats in an election than before?
35212.e: If a party gets more seats than at the last election, people speak of a seat gain. If it loses seats, it is a seat loss.
35212.m: More seats than before is called a seat gain.

35213.q: What does an election winner often do on election evening?
a: Throws the posters into the water
35213.e: On election evening, many of those elected thank everyone who voted for them and supported them.

35214.q: How many seats in the National Council did the SVP have after the 2023 election?
35214.e: In 2023 the SVP won 62 of the 200 seats. That makes it the largest parliamentary group in the National Council.
35214.m: Since the 2023 election the SVP has had 62 seats in the National Council.

35215.q: Does the election winner in Switzerland have to govern alone?
a: No, several parties are in the Federal Council
35215.e: In Switzerland, several large parties sit together in the Federal Council. No party governs alone.
35215.m: In Switzerland several parties govern together.

a: When you vote for the first time
35216.e: In a re-election, someone who is already in office gets the votes again. That way he or she can carry on.
35216.m: In a re-election someone may stay in office.

35217.q: What is it called when someone in office is not re-elected?
35217.e: When someone is voted out, they lose their office because they get too few votes. This happens to incumbents too.
35217.m: Anyone who is not re-elected has been voted out.

35218.q: How many times may you be re-elected to the National Council in Switzerland?
35218.e: Federal law sets no limit for the National Council. But some parties have their own rules on how long members may serve.
35218.m: There is no legal limit on re-election to the National Council.

35219.q: What is the maximum number of times a President of the USA may be elected?
35219.e: Since 1951 a rule in the US Constitution has applied. A President may be elected no more than twice.
35219.m: In the USA you may be elected President no more than twice.

35220.q: What advantage do incumbents often have in an election?
a: They do not have to stand
They may count on their own
35220.e: Incumbents are already known and have often been in the media. This usually helps them to get re-elected.
35220.m: Incumbents are often better known than new candidates.

35221.q: Who stands for re-election in the general election of the Federal Council?
a: The current Federal Councillors who want to carry on
35221.e: In the general election all seven seats are filled again. Anyone who wants to carry on stands for re-election.
35221.m: Federal Councillors who want to carry on stand for re-election.

35222.q: What must a National Councillor do if she wants to carry on after four years?
35222.e: After four years the whole National Council is elected again. Anyone who wants to stay must stand again and get enough votes.
35222.m: Anyone who wants to stay in office must stand again.

35223.q: What does a re-election show about a person's work?
35223.e: Anyone who is re-elected has enough support. Many voters want her to carry on.
35223.m: A re-election shows the voters' trust.

35224.e: On election evening, party members and friends meet. They wait for the results together.
35224.m: At an election party people wait for the results together.

35225.q: When does an election party usually take place?
a: On the evening of election day
On the morning before the election
35225.e: The results come on election Sunday. That is why parties usually celebrate on the afternoon and evening of that day.
35225.m: Election parties take place on election day.

35226.q: Why do people cheer at an election party?
a: Because there is a power cut
35226.e: When good results come in, everyone is happy. They cheer, clap and congratulate those elected.
35226.m: At the election party people cheer about good results.

35227.q: What do guests at an election party often follow on a big screen?
35227.e: At many election parties the election programme is on television. That way you see the new figures straight away.
35227.m: At the election party you follow the results on screen.

35228.q: Who often comes to a party's election party?
35228.e: At the election party, candidates, party members and helpers meet. They worked together in the campaign.
35228.m: At the election party everyone who helped in the campaign meets.

35229.q: How do you behave at an election party if your own party has lost?
a: You comfort each other and stay fair
35229.e: A defeat is also part of democracy. You stay fair and think about the next election.
35229.m: Even after a defeat you stay fair.

35230.q: Who often comes to the election party on election evening to ask questions?
35230.e: Journalists want to know how those elected feel. They do interviews for television, radio and newspapers.
35230.m: On election evening those elected often give interviews.

35231.q: Where do election parties often take place?
35231.e: An election party needs room for lots of people. The party often hires a hall or a restaurant.
35231.m: Election parties often take place in a hall or restaurant.

35232.q: In how many cantons may you stand for the National Council at the same time?
35232.e: In the National Council election, a person may only be on a list in one single canton. Usually this is the canton where they live.
35232.m: You stand for the National Council in only one canton.

35233.q: What is paid election advertising in a newspaper called?
35233.e: An advert is a paid announcement. In the election campaign, parties and candidates buy space in newspapers.
35233.m: An advert is paid advertising in the newspaper.

35234.q: Which other election takes place on the same day as the National Council election in most cantons?
a: The election of the President of the Confederation
The election of the federal judges
35234.e: Almost all cantons elect their members of the Council of States on the same Sunday as the National Council. The Federal Council and the federal judges, on the other hand, are elected by Parliament.
35234.m: The National Council and the Council of States are usually elected on the same day.

35235.q: What is the municipality's list in which all people entitled to vote are registered called?
35235.e: The electoral register contains everyone who may vote in the municipality. Only those registered there get the voting papers.
35235.m: People entitled to vote are in the municipality's electoral register.

35236.q: How old did you used to have to be to vote at federal level in Switzerland?
35236.e: In the past you could only vote at federal level from the age of 20. Today the voting age is lower.
35236.m: In the past you could only vote from the age of 20.

35237.q: In which year did the people accept the voting age of 18 for the whole of Switzerland?
35237.e: On 3 March 1991 the voters said Yes to a voting age of 18. Since then all Swiss citizens aged 18 and over may take part at federal level.
35237.m: Since 1991 the voting age at federal level has been 18.

35238.q: What is the right to say Yes or No in a vote called?
35238.e: With the right to vote you may give your opinion in votes with Yes or No. It is one of the political rights.
35238.m: The right to vote lets you say Yes or No.

35239.q: What is the right to elect people to a political office called?
35239.e: With the right to elect, voters decide who sits, for example, in the National Council. The right to elect and the right to vote belong together.
35239.m: With the right to elect you decide who gets an office.

35240.q: In which canton must voters vote, or else pay a small fine?
35240.e: In the canton of Schaffhausen there is compulsory voting. Anyone who does not vote without a good reason has to pay a small amount.
35240.m: There is compulsory voting in Schaffhausen.

35241.q: Do you have to tell other people how you voted?
35241.e: In ballot box votes the secrecy of the vote applies. Nobody may demand that you reveal your vote.
35241.m: You may keep to yourself how you voted.

35242.q: From what age can you be elected to the National Council?
35242.e: Anyone who may vote and elect at federal level can also be elected to the National Council. That is from the age of 18.
35242.m: You can become a National Councillor at just 18.

35243.q: How does the voting card reach voters?
35243.e: The municipality sends the voting papers with the voting card by post a few weeks before voting day. That way everyone can prepare.
35243.m: The voting card comes by post.

35244.q: In most cantons, what must you do with the voting card when you vote by post?
35244.e: With your signature you confirm that you voted yourself. Without a signature, the vote does not count in many cantons.
35244.m: When voting by post you sign the voting card.

35245.q: Who sends out the voting card?
35245.e: The municipality knows who lives there and may vote. That is why it sends the papers to all voters.
35245.m: The municipality sends out the voting cards.

35246.q: When voting by post, where do you put the filled-in ballot paper?
35246.e: The ballot paper goes into a small ballot envelope, which you seal. That way how you voted stays secret.
35246.m: The ballot paper goes into the ballot envelope.

35247.q: What is the box you put your ballot paper into at the polling station called?
35247.e: At the polling station you put your ballot paper into a locked ballot box. That is why people also speak of a ballot box vote.
35247.m: You put the ballot paper into the ballot box.

35248.q: What do you take with you if you want to vote at the polling station on Sunday?
35248.e: At the polling station you show your voting card. That shows that you are entitled to vote.
35248.m: You take your voting card to the polling station.

35249.q: What is it called when you send the voting papers back by post?
35249.e: With postal voting you send the papers by post or put them in the municipality's letterbox. Most people vote this way today.

35250.q: What is the booklet with explanations that you get with the voting papers called?
35250.e: In the voting booklet the Federal Council explains the proposals. The opinions of the supporters and opponents are in it too.
35250.m: The voting booklet explains the proposals.

35251.q: In which canton may 16-year-olds already take part in cantonal votes?
35251.e: In 2007 the canton of Glarus became the first and so far only canton to introduce a voting age of 16. There, young people aged 16 and over may have a say in the canton.
35251.m: In Glarus young people may vote from the age of 16.

35252.q: May a 16-year-old from Glarus take part in votes for the whole of Switzerland?
35252.e: The voting age of 16 in Glarus only applies to the canton and the municipalities. At federal level you may only vote from 18 everywhere.
35252.m: At federal level the voting age of 18 applies to people from Glarus too.

35253.q: What is the open-air assembly in Glarus at which 16-year-olds may also vote called?
35253.e: At the Glarus Landsgemeinde, voters vote outdoors every year by raising their hands. 16- and 17-year-olds may also take part.
35253.m: At the Glarus Landsgemeinde, 16-year-olds vote too.

35254.q: In which of Switzerland's neighbouring countries can you already elect the national parliament at 16?
35254.e: In Austria the voting age of 16 has applied to all elections since 2007. In Germany, France and Italy people elect the parliament from 18.
35254.m: In Austria people vote from the age of 16.

35255.q: What do you call the age from which you may vote?
35255.e: The voting age says how old you must be to be allowed to vote. In Switzerland it is 18 at federal level.
35255.m: The voting age sets from when you may vote.

35256.q: How many years earlier than at federal level may young people in Glarus vote in the canton?
35256.e: At federal level the voting age is 18; in the canton of Glarus it is 16. The sum is 18 minus 16 = 2.
35256.m: Young people in Glarus vote in the canton two years earlier.

35257.q: What did voters in the cantons of Bern and Zurich say in 2022 about a voting age of 16?
35257.e: In 2022 voters in Bern and Zurich rejected a voting age of 16. There it is still 18.
35257.m: In Bern and Zurich a voting age of 16 was rejected.

35258.q: Who must say Yes in a canton for a voting age of 16 to be introduced there?
35258.e: The voting age is in the cantonal constitution. A change to the constitution must be accepted by the voters.
35258.m: The people decide on a lower voting age.

a: All young people in the world
35259.e: In Glarus too, you need Swiss citizenship and residence in the canton to vote. Young people without a Swiss passport may not vote.
35259.m: In Glarus too, you need a Swiss passport to vote.

35260.q: Who was allowed to vote on women's suffrage at federal level in 1971?
a: All the people in the world
35260.e: Before 1971 only men had the right to vote at federal level. So the men had to decide whether women could vote too.
35260.m: In 1971 the men decided on women's suffrage.

35261.q: How many of the men voting in 1971 said Yes to women's suffrage?
35261.e: On 7 February 1971 around 66 per cent said Yes. That is about two thirds of the votes.
35261.m: In 1971 two thirds of the votes were in favour of women's suffrage.

35262.q: In which month of 1971 was the vote on women's suffrage held?
35262.e: The vote took place on 7 February 1971. Since that day women may vote and stand for election at federal level.
35262.m: In February 1971 women got the right to vote.

35263.q: In which year did men first say No to women's suffrage at federal level?
35263.e: In the first vote in 1959, men clearly rejected women's suffrage. It only succeeded in 1971.
35263.m: The first attempt at women's suffrage failed in 1959.

35264.q: How many years after the men (1848) did women get the right to vote at federal level in 1971?
35264.e: You calculate 1971 minus 1848 = 123. That is how long women had to wait for the right to vote at federal level.
35264.m: Women waited 123 years longer than men.

35265.q: What were women in Switzerland not yet allowed to do at federal level before 1971?
35265.e: Before 1971 women had no right to vote or stand for election at federal level. But they were already allowed to learn, study and have a bank account.
35265.m: Before 1971 women were not allowed to vote at federal level.

35266.q: Which country in Europe gave women the full right to vote as early as 1906?
35266.e: In 1906 Finland was the first country in Europe with the full right to vote and stand for election for women. Switzerland only followed much later.
35266.m: Finland led the way in Europe on women's suffrage.

35267.q: What were the women in England who campaigned loudly for women's suffrage called?
35267.e: The suffragettes campaigned in England more than 100 years ago for women's right to vote. The word comes from “suffrage”, meaning the right to vote.
35267.m: The suffragettes fought for women's right to vote.

35268.q: Does a child automatically become Swiss just because they were born in Switzerland?
35268.e: In Switzerland a child gets citizenship through its parents. Place of birth alone does not make anyone Swiss.
35268.m: You get Swiss citizenship through your parents.

35269.q: What colour is the Swiss passport?
35269.e: The Swiss passport is red and has a white cross. It shows that you have Swiss citizenship.

35270.q: What do you call a person who has the citizenship of two countries?
35270.e: Switzerland allows people to have two or more citizenships. Such people are called dual citizens.
35270.m: Dual citizens have the citizenship of two countries.

35271.q: At how many levels does a Swiss citizen have citizenship?
35271.e: You have citizenship of a municipality, a canton and Switzerland. These three levels belong together.
35271.m: Swiss citizenship applies to the municipality, the canton and the Confederation.

35272.q: What duty do young Swiss men have?
35272.e: Swiss men must do military service or civilian service. Anyone who does not do service pays an exemption tax.
35272.m: Swiss men do military or civilian service.

35273.q: What is the small plastic ID for Swiss citizens called?
35273.e: Besides the passport there is the identity card in card format. You can use it to travel to many countries in Europe.
35273.m: The identity card is an ID in card format.

35274.q: What may only adults with Swiss citizenship do at federal level?
35274.e: For the right to vote and elect at federal level you need Swiss citizenship and must be 18. All children may go to school.
35274.m: At federal level only Swiss citizens vote.

35275.q: What do you need to be elected to the Federal Council?
35275.e: Anyone entitled to vote at federal level can be elected to the Federal Council. For this you need Swiss citizenship.
35275.m: Federal Councillors must have Swiss citizenship.

35276.q: How many years must you usually have lived in Switzerland before you can apply for naturalisation?
35276.e: For ordinary naturalisation you usually need to have lived in Switzerland for 10 years. There are other conditions too.
35276.m: Naturalisation usually requires 10 years in Switzerland.

35277.q: Which years count double for naturalisation?
35277.e: If you live in Switzerland as a child and teenager between 8 and 18, these years count double. But you must still have actually lived here for at least 6 years.
35277.m: Childhood years between 8 and 18 count double for naturalisation.

35278.q: Who has a say in an ordinary naturalisation?
35278.e: In an ordinary naturalisation, the municipality, the canton and the Confederation examine the application. All three must agree.
35278.m: The municipality, canton and Confederation all have a say in naturalisation.

35279.q: What must you be good at for naturalisation in Switzerland?
35279.e: Anyone who wants to be naturalised must be able to speak and write a national language. This can be German, French, Italian or Romansh.
35279.m: For naturalisation you must know a national language.

35280.q: What is the simpler naturalisation, for example for spouses of Swiss citizens, called?
35280.e: Spouses of Swiss citizens can obtain simplified naturalisation under certain conditions. The Confederation decides on this.
35280.m: There is simplified naturalisation for spouses.

35281.q: For whom did the people make naturalisation easier in 2017?
35281.e: In February 2017 the people said Yes to simplified naturalisation for the third generation. These are young people whose grandparents immigrated.
35281.m: Young foreigners of the third generation can be naturalised more easily.

35282.q: What do municipalities often test in naturalisation?
35282.e: In naturalisation you have to show that you know Switzerland. Often there is a test or an interview about history, politics and the municipality.
35282.m: In naturalisation you show that you know Switzerland.

35283.q: Which country does the largest group of foreigners in Switzerland come from (as of 2024)?
35283.e: More than 300,000 people with an Italian passport live in Switzerland. They are the largest foreign group.
35283.m: The largest foreign group in Switzerland comes from Italy.

35284.q: In which two cantons may foreigners also take part in cantonal votes?
35284.e: In Neuchâtel and Jura, foreigners who have lived there a long time may also vote in the canton. In most other cantons this is not possible.
35284.m: Neuchâtel and Jura let foreigners vote in the canton.

35285.q: May foreigners without a Swiss passport take part in federal votes?
35285.e: At federal level only Swiss citizens may vote. Anyone without a Swiss passport may not take part.
35285.m: Without a Swiss passport you do not vote at federal level.

35286.q: Which permit do foreigners often get when they first come to Switzerland to work?
35286.e: Permit B is the residence permit. Anyone who has lived here for a long time can later get permit C.
35286.m: Many foreigners first get permit B.

35287.q: In which canton may foreigners vote in the municipalities but not in the canton?
35287.e: In the canton of Vaud, foreigners who have lived there a long time may vote and stand in municipal elections. They may not take part in cantonal votes.
35287.m: In Vaud foreigners have a say in the municipality.

35288.q: What do you call a person who moves to Switzerland from another country?
35288.e: An immigrant moves to a new country to live there. An emigrant leaves their country.
35288.m: Anyone who moves to Switzerland is an immigrant.

35289.q: What do you call people who have to flee their country because of war?
35289.e: Refugees leave their home because they are in danger there. Switzerland takes in refugees and protects them.
35289.m: Refugees flee their home because of danger.

35290.q: How many Swiss citizens live abroad (as of 2024)?
35290.e: At the end of 2024 around 826,700 Swiss citizens lived abroad. Their number grows every year.

35291.q: In which country do the most Swiss citizens abroad live (as of 2024)?
35291.e: Around 212,000 Swiss citizens abroad live in France. No other country has so many Swiss citizens abroad.
35291.m: Most Swiss citizens abroad live in France.

35292.q: What else are the Swiss citizens abroad called?
35292.e: In addition to the four language regions, the Swiss abroad are called the “Fifth Switzerland”. This shows that they belong.
35292.m: The Swiss abroad are also called the Fifth Switzerland.

35293.q: Where do Swiss citizens abroad register so that they can vote in Switzerland?
a: At the Swiss embassy or consulate
At the Federal Palace in Bern
At the municipality in their new country
At the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
35293.e: Swiss citizens abroad register with the Swiss representation in their country. Then they can have themselves entered for the right to vote.
35293.m: Swiss citizens abroad register with the Swiss representation.

35294.q: On which continent do about two thirds of the Swiss abroad live?
35294.e: Around 530,000 Swiss citizens abroad live in Europe. That is about two thirds of them all.
35294.m: Most Swiss citizens abroad live in Europe.

35295.q: What is the organisation that works for the Swiss abroad called?
35295.e: The Organisation of the Swiss Abroad, OSA for short, helps Swiss people abroad. It represents their interests in Switzerland.
35295.m: The OSA works for the Swiss abroad.

35296.q: What do you call a person who moves from Switzerland to another country?
35296.e: Anyone who leaves Switzerland to live abroad is an emigrant. In the new country they are then an immigrant.

35297.q: Many Swiss citizens abroad have two passports. What are such people called?
35297.e: About three quarters of the Swiss abroad have another nationality besides their Swiss passport. They are dual citizens.
35297.m: Most Swiss citizens abroad are dual citizens.

35298.q: At what age do you come of age in Switzerland?
35298.e: In Switzerland you come of age at 18. Then you may decide many things for yourself.

35299.q: At what age did you use to come of age in Switzerland?
35299.e: In the past you only came of age in Switzerland at 20. Later the age was lowered to 18.
35299.m: In the past you only came of age at 20.

35300.q: Since which year have people in Switzerland come of age at 18?
35300.e: Since 1 January 1996 the age of majority in Switzerland has been 18. Since then young adults may decide for themselves much earlier.
35300.m: Since 1996 you have come of age at 18.

35301.q: What may you do from 18 without your parents' permission?
35301.e: Adults may enter into contracts themselves, for example for a flat. Before that you often need your parents' consent.

35302.q: What do you call a person who is not yet 18?
35302.e: Anyone who is not yet 18 is a minor. For many things you then need your parents' permission.

35303.q: Who usually decides on important things for children who are minors?
35303.e: For children, the parents usually have parental responsibility. They decide on important things, but listen to the child.
35303.m: For children, the parents usually decide on important things.

35304.q: From what age may you marry in Switzerland?
35304.e: In Switzerland you may only marry when you are 18. Even with your parents' permission it is not possible earlier.
35304.m: In Switzerland you may only marry at 18.

35306.e: Children may not vote in Switzerland yet. There is a minimum age for the right to vote.

35307.q: How can children still think along about a vote?
a: Talk to their parents about the proposals
Fill in their parents' ballot paper
35307.e: Children may talk about votes with their family and say what they think. But voters fill in their ballot papers themselves.
35307.m: Children can talk about votes and say what they think.

35308.q: Does a family with three children have more votes in a vote?
35308.e: Every person entitled to vote has one vote. Children do not have a vote yet, so the number of children does not count.
35308.m: Children do not give their parents extra votes.

35309.q: Why may children not vote yet?
a: The law sets a minimum age
35309.e: The law sets the age from which you may vote. Children still have an opinion and may say it.
35309.m: A minimum age sets when you may vote.

35310.q: What is the group of pupils who have a say for the whole school called?
35310.e: The school council has children from different classes. They bring in the pupils' ideas and wishes.
35310.m: The school council speaks up for the children of the school.

35311.q: Where can children already practise voting today?
35311.e: In the class council, children discuss problems in the class and vote. This way they practise deciding together.
35311.m: In the class council children practise having a say.

35312.q: What is it called when children may have a say in a decision?
35312.e: Anyone who participates may give their opinion and have a say in the decision. Many schools and municipalities let children participate.
35312.m: When participating, children have a say in decisions.

35313.q: What is the celebration to which many municipalities invite young people at 18 called?
35313.e: At the new citizens' celebration the municipality welcomes the new voters. There is often a meal and information about politics.
35313.m: At the new citizens' celebration new voters are welcomed.

35314.q: What is a good way to form an opinion before a vote?
35314.e: If you know different opinions, you can decide better. Newspapers, the voting booklet and conversations help with this.
35314.m: Before a vote it is best to listen to different opinions.

35315.q: From what age may you vote in Switzerland?
35315.e: In Switzerland you may vote and elect from 18. In the canton of Glarus this is already possible from 16 in cantonal votes.
35315.m: In Switzerland you may vote from 18.

35316.q: What does equality of rights mean?
a: Everyone lives in the same house
35316.e: Equality of rights means that all people have the same rights. Nobody may be disadvantaged because of their sex or origin.
35316.m: Equality of rights means the same rights for everyone.

35317.q: Since which year has equality between women and men been in the Federal Constitution?
35317.e: On 14 June 1981 the people accepted the equality article. Since then the Constitution has said that men and women have equal rights.
35317.m: Since 1981 equality has been in the Federal Constitution.

35318.q: What should women and men get for the same work?
35318.e: The Federal Constitution requires equal pay for work of equal value. This applies to women and men.
35318.m: The same work gets the same pay.

35319.q: What is the 1996 law that protects women from being disadvantaged at work called?
35319.e: The Gender Equality Act has applied since 1996. It forbids disadvantaging women and men at work because of their sex.
35319.m: The Gender Equality Act protects against being disadvantaged at work.

35320.q: According to the Federal Constitution, because of what may nobody be disadvantaged?
35320.e: The Federal Constitution forbids discrimination, for example because of sex, origin, language or religion. All people are equal before the law.
35320.m: Nobody may be disadvantaged because of their sex.

35321.q: Which colour did many women wear at the women's strike in 2019?
35321.e: At the women's strike on 14 June 2019 many participants wore purple. The colour is a symbol of the women's movement.
35321.m: Purple is the colour of the women's strike.

35322.q: What do you call the people who may take part in a vote?
35322.e: Anyone who has the right to vote is a voter. At federal level these are Swiss citizens aged 18 and over.
35322.m: Anyone who may vote is a voter.

35323.q: Roughly how many people are entitled to vote at federal level (as of 2023)?
35323.e: In the 2023 elections around 5.6 million people were entitled to vote, including the Swiss abroad. Children and foreigners are not included.
35323.m: Switzerland has over five million people entitled to vote.

35324.q: What does the municipality send a young Swiss woman for the first time shortly after her 18th birthday?
35324.e: At 18 you become entitled to vote at federal level. That is why before the next vote you get your own voting papers for the first time.
35324.m: At 18 you get your first own voting papers.

35325.q: Which permit can foreigners who have lived in Switzerland for a long time get?
35325.e: Permit C is called the settlement permit. You usually get it after 5 or 10 years in Switzerland.
35325.m: Anyone who has lived here a long time can get permit C.

35326.q: What do you call people who live abroad and come to Switzerland to work?
35326.e: Cross-border commuters live, for example, in France, Italy or Germany. They travel regularly to work in Switzerland.
35326.m: Cross-border commuters live abroad and work in Switzerland.

35327.q: Who in Switzerland votes on things that affect children, for example a new school building?
35327.e: On questions about schools too, the voters decide. But children can put forward their wishes beforehand.

35328.q: What is the school subject in which you learn how votes and elections work called?
35328.e: In civics you learn how Switzerland is governed. That way you are well prepared when you are allowed to have a say later.
35328.m: In civics you learn how politics works.

35329.q: What is it called when you work for others without pay, for example in a club?
35329.e: Many people in Switzerland volunteer in clubs, in the neighbourhood or with the fire brigade. That way they help shape life in the municipality.
35329.m: Voluntary work is helping others without pay.

35330.q: May Swiss women do military service?
35330.e: For Swiss men, service is compulsory. Women may do military service voluntarily and then have the same tasks.
35330.m: In Switzerland women do military service voluntarily.

35331.q: How many years had women had the right to vote at federal level in 2021?
35331.e: Women have been able to vote at federal level since 1971. You work it out like this: 2021 minus 1971 = 50.
35331.m: In 2021, Switzerland celebrated 50 years of votes for women.

35332.q: In which neighbouring country do the second most Swiss abroad live (as of 2024)?
35332.e: Around 101,000 Swiss citizens abroad live in Germany. That puts Germany in second place.
35332.m: Many Swiss abroad live in Germany.

35333.q: Which document can you apply for after naturalisation?
35333.e: After naturalisation you are a Swiss citizen. Then you can apply for a Swiss passport and an identity card.
35333.m: After naturalisation you get the Swiss passport.

35334.q: What can you do with a popular initiative?
35334.e: With a popular initiative, citizens propose a new rule. Then the whole people vote on it.
35334.m: With a popular initiative, the people make a proposal.

35335.e: A popular initiative comes from the people. People who are entitled to vote join together and submit their idea.
35335.m: A popular initiative comes from the people.

35336.q: What does a federal popular initiative change?
35336.e: A popular initiative for the whole of Switzerland aims to change the Federal Constitution. The constitution is the country's most important law.
35336.m: A federal popular initiative aims to change the Federal Constitution.

35337.q: What happens in the end with a valid popular initiative?
a: The Federal Council tears it up
35337.e: When a popular initiative has succeeded, there is a popular vote. Then the voters decide with Yes or No.
35337.m: The people vote on a valid popular initiative.

35338.q: Since when has the popular initiative existed for the whole of Switzerland?
35338.e: The popular initiative at federal level was introduced in 1891. So it is more than 130 years old.
35338.m: The popular initiative has existed in Switzerland since 1891.

35339.q: What do most people mean when they talk about an “initiative” in Swiss politics?
35339.e: In everyday life people often just say “initiative”. They usually mean a popular initiative.
35339.m: Instead of popular initiative, people often just say initiative.

35340.q: Who may vote on a federal popular initiative?
35340.e: Swiss citizens aged 18 and over may vote. They are called voters, or people entitled to vote.
35340.m: The voters vote on a popular initiative.

35341.q: What does a popular initiative show about Switzerland?
a: The people have a big say
Only rich people have a say
35341.e: In Switzerland the people can put forward new ideas themselves. This is called direct democracy.
35341.m: The popular initiative is part of direct democracy.

35342.q: A group collects 10,000 valid signatures every month. After how many months does it have enough for a popular initiative?
35342.e: 100,000 signatures are needed. 100,000 divided by 10,000 is 10, so 10 months.
35342.m: With 10,000 signatures a month, it takes 10 months to reach 100,000.

35343.q: A group has 80,000 valid signatures for an initiative. Is that enough?
35343.e: 100,000 signatures are needed. 100,000 minus 80,000 leaves 20,000 still missing.
35343.m: With fewer than 100,000 signatures, an initiative does not succeed.

35344.q: How do you write “one hundred thousand” as a number?
35344.e: One hundred thousand is a 1 followed by five zeros. That is how many signatures a popular initiative needs.
35344.m: One hundred thousand is written as a 1 with five zeros.

35345.q: What happens to an initiative that has too few signatures at the end of the deadline?
a: The Federal Council pays for the rest
35345.e: If valid signatures are missing at the end of the collection period, the initiative does not succeed. There is then no vote.
35345.m: Without enough signatures, an initiative fails.

35346.e: A year has 12 months. 12 + 6 makes 18, so one and a half years.
35346.m: 18 months are one and a half years.

35347.q: Why do initiatives often collect more than 100,000 signatures?
35347.e: Some signatures are invalid, for example if someone is not entitled to vote. That is why people prefer to collect a few more.
35347.m: People collect extra signatures because some are invalid.

35348.q: What does it mean when an initiative has “qualified”?
a: The people have already said Yes
35348.e: “Qualified” means there are enough valid signatures. Only after that does the vote follow.
35348.m: An initiative has qualified when there are enough valid signatures.

35349.q: May you also submit a popular initiative with 150,000 signatures?
35349.e: At least 100,000 valid signatures are needed. More signatures are allowed.
35349.m: For an initiative, 100,000 signatures are the minimum.

35350.q: What do you sign for a popular initiative?
35350.e: For an initiative you sign a list called the signature form. The municipality then checks every signature.
35350.m: For an initiative you sign a signature form.

35351.q: What do you write on the signature form next to your signature?
35351.e: The form asks for surname, first name and address. Then comes your own signature.
35351.m: The signature form has your name, address and signature.

35352.q: What text is at the top of an initiative's signature form?
a: Title and text of the initiative
35352.e: The form shows the title and the exact text of the initiative. That way you know what you are signing for.
35352.m: The form says what you are signing for.

35353.q: Which date must you give on the signature form?
a: The date of your dentist appointment
35353.e: On the form you give your date of birth. This lets the municipality check who has signed.
35353.m: The signature form includes your date of birth.

35354.q: Who may sign on the same signature form?
a: People from all over the world
35354.e: Only people from the same political municipality may sign on one form. The municipality then checks its own residents.
35354.m: A signature form is for one single municipality.

35355.q: Who checks on the form whether someone is entitled to vote?
35355.e: The municipality where the person lives checks that they live there and may vote. It confirms this on the form.
35355.m: The municipality confirms that someone is entitled to vote.

35356.q: How must you sign the form?
35356.e: Each person must sign themselves, by hand. Nobody may sign for someone else.
35356.m: Everyone signs the form themselves, by hand.

35357.q: How often may you sign for the same initiative?
35357.e: Each person may sign only once for the same initiative. Double signatures are invalid.
35357.m: You sign only once for the same initiative.

35358.q: Where do people often collect signatures for an initiative?
35358.e: Many collectors stand in squares and streets. There they talk to people and ask for a signature.
35358.m: Signatures are often collected in the street.

35359.q: What do signature collectors in the street usually have with them?
35359.e: To collect signatures you need signature forms and something to write with. Often there is also a small stand.
35359.m: Collectors have forms and a pen with them.

35360.q: Do you have to sign when a collector asks you?
a: Yes, or you get a fine
35360.e: Signing is voluntary. If you do not agree with the idea, you can simply say no.

35361.q: Apart from in the street, how else can you get a signature form?
a: Collect it from the lost property office
35361.e: Many committees put their forms online. You print the form, sign it and post it back.
35361.m: You can often print a form from the internet.

35362.q: May a 9-year-old child sign a federal initiative?
35362.e: Only people entitled to vote may sign. In Switzerland you are entitled to vote from the age of 18.
35362.m: You may sign an initiative from the age of 18.

35363.q: What is forbidden when collecting signatures?
35363.e: Anyone who forges signatures commits a crime. Every signature form also points this out.

35364.q: Why do collectors explain their idea to people?
a: So they sign because they are convinced
35364.e: People who understand an idea and like it are more likely to sign. That is why collectors briefly explain what it is about.
35364.m: Collectors explain their idea so people are happy to sign.

35365.q: What do you do with the completed signature form?
35365.e: The completed form goes back to the committee. Only then can the signature be counted.
35365.m: You send a completed form back to the committee.

35366.q: What can you achieve with a referendum?
35366.e: With a referendum you demand that the people vote on a new law. Then the people decide whether it applies.
35366.m: With a referendum, the people vote on a law.

35367.q: Who makes the laws in Switzerland that you can challenge with a referendum?
35367.e: The Federal Assembly is the Swiss parliament. It passes new laws, and a referendum is possible against them.
35367.m: Parliament makes laws, and the people can check them with a referendum.

35368.q: Which referendum always takes place without signatures?
35368.e: If the Federal Constitution changes, the people must always vote. This is called a mandatory referendum.
35368.m: When the constitution changes, the people always vote.

35369.q: What does the word “optional” mean in the optional referendum?
35369.e: “Optional” means it only happens if someone demands it. This requires signatures.
35369.m: An optional referendum only happens if someone demands it.

35370.q: Who can demand a referendum against a federal law?
a: Only the President of the Confederation
35370.e: A referendum can be demanded by 50,000 voters or 8 cantons. Usually groups collect signatures.
35370.m: Voters or cantons can demand a referendum.

35371.q: Which referendum only happens if enough signatures are collected?
35371.e: In an optional referendum, a vote only takes place if 50,000 voters or 8 cantons demand it. Optional means voluntary.

35372.q: Are there referendums in cantons and municipalities too?
35372.e: Cantons and many municipalities also have the referendum. The rules and numbers of signatures vary there.
35372.m: Referendums exist at federal level, in cantons and in municipalities.

35373.q: What happens to a new law if nobody launches a referendum?
35373.e: If no referendum succeeds within the deadline, the law simply applies. There is then no vote.
35373.m: Without a referendum, a new law comes into force.

35374.q: What is it called when at least 8 cantons demand a popular vote on a federal law?
35374.e: Cantons can also demand a referendum. The cantonal referendum has only succeeded once so far, in 2003 against a federal tax package.
35374.m: At least 8 cantons can demand a cantonal referendum.

35375.q: A referendum needs 50,000 signatures in 100 days. How many is that on average per day?
35375.e: 50,000 divided by 100 is 500. So you have to collect about 500 signatures every day.
35375.m: A referendum needs an average of 500 signatures a day.

35376.q: From when does the 100-day deadline for a referendum run?
a: From the publication of the law
From the start of the next session
35376.e: The collection period begins when the new law is published in the Federal Gazette. From then on the days count.
35376.m: The referendum deadline begins with the publication of the law.

35377.e: 100,000 divided by 2 is 50,000. That is how many signatures a referendum needs.

35378.e: An initiative needs 100,000 signatures, a referendum 50,000. So the initiative needs more.
35378.m: An initiative needs more signatures than a referendum.

35379.q: A referendum has 60,000 valid signatures. Has it qualified?
35379.e: A referendum needs 50,000 signatures. 60,000 is more, so it is enough.
35379.m: With at least 50,000 signatures, a referendum qualifies.

35380.q: A committee has 45,000 valid signatures for a referendum. How many are missing?
35380.m: A referendum needs at least 50,000 signatures.

35381.q: How long do you have to collect signatures for a referendum?
35381.e: For a referendum you only have 100 days, a little over three months. For a popular initiative it is 18 months.
35381.m: The collection period is shorter for a referendum than for an initiative.

35382.q: Who establishes whether a referendum against a federal law has enough signatures?
35382.e: The signatures for a referendum go to the Federal Chancellery. It checks whether there are enough valid ones.
35382.m: The Federal Chancellery also checks the signatures for a referendum.

35383.q: Which area does a federal popular initiative apply to?
35383.e: “Federal” means it concerns the whole of Switzerland. Such an initiative wants a rule for the entire country.
35383.m: A federal initiative applies to the whole of Switzerland.

35384.q: Can a citizen entitled to vote bring an idea for the whole country to a vote?
a: No, only the Federal Council may
Only as a member of parliament
35384.e: With a popular initiative, any person entitled to vote can put forward an idea. They need a committee and enough signatures.
35384.m: With enough signatures, anyone entitled to vote can put forward an idea for the whole country.

35385.q: Which majorities does a federal popular initiative need?
35385.e: A federal initiative needs a Yes from the majority of the people and the majority of the cantons. This is called the popular majority and the cantonal majority.
35385.m: An initiative needs the popular majority and the cantonal majority.

35386.q: What is the popular initiative for a single canton called?
35386.e: There are popular initiatives in the cantons too. They are called cantonal popular initiatives and apply only to that canton.
35386.m: A cantonal popular initiative applies to one canton only.

35387.q: How many topics may a popular initiative cover?
35387.e: An initiative must respect the unity of subject matter. It may only deal with one topic, otherwise parliament can declare it invalid.
35387.m: A popular initiative may only deal with one topic.

35388.q: What was the first federal popular initiative to be accepted?
a: The ban on slaughter without stunning, 1893
35388.e: In 1893 the people accepted their first initiative: a ban on slaughtering animals without stunning them first.
35388.m: The first accepted popular initiative was the 1893 ban on slaughter without stunning.

35389.q: How often does a federal popular initiative get through with the people?
35389.e: Most federal popular initiatives are rejected. Only a small share is accepted.
35389.m: Most popular initiatives are rejected by the people.

35390.q: Where is an accepted federal popular initiative written down?
35390.e: If an initiative is accepted, its text goes into the Federal Constitution. Afterwards parliament often makes matching laws.
35390.m: An accepted initiative goes into the Federal Constitution.

35391.q: What is an optional referendum for?
a: Being able to reject a law
35391.e: With an optional referendum, the people can reject a new law. First, enough signatures are needed.
35391.m: With a referendum, the people can reject a law.

35392.q: In a referendum, the majority of the people say No. What happens to the law?
a: It does not come into force
35392.e: If the majority say No, the law is rejected. It then does not come into force.
35392.m: After a No, the law does not come into force.

35393.q: What can an association do if it does not like a new federal law?
35393.e: Anyone who opposes a new law can collect signatures and launch a referendum. Then the people decide.
35393.m: You can launch a referendum against an unpopular law.

35394.q: Who often collects signatures against a new law?
35394.e: Often it is parties, associations or groups of citizens. They do not agree with the law.
35394.m: Parties or associations often collect signatures against a law.

35395.q: In an optional referendum, does a federal law also need a Yes from the majority of the cantons?
a: No, the popular majority is enough
Yes, it needs people and cantons
Yes, but only the large cantons
35395.e: In an optional referendum the majority of voters decides. The cantonal majority is not needed there.
35395.m: In an optional referendum only the popular majority counts.

35396.q: In a referendum, what does a “Yes” on the ballot paper mean?
a: I do not want the law
I want parliament to discuss it again
35396.e: In the vote, the question is whether you want to accept the law. So a Yes means the law should apply.
35396.m: A Yes in a referendum means the law should apply.

35397.q: When do you launch a referendum?
35397.e: First parliament passes a law. Only after that can you launch a referendum against it.
35397.m: You launch a referendum after parliament has passed a law.

35398.q: What is the group that organises a referendum called?
35398.e: Anyone who launches a referendum usually forms a referendum committee. It organises the collection of signatures.
35398.m: A referendum committee organises the campaign against a law.

35399.q: Which language does the word “petition” come from?
35399.e: “Petition” comes from the Latin word “petitio”. It means a request or plea.
35399.m: The word petition comes from Latin and means request.

35400.q: Can you also collect a petition on the internet?
35400.e: There are no strict formal rules for a petition. That is why many petitions are collected online today.
35400.m: You can also collect a petition online.

35401.q: What is the minimum number of signatures a petition needs?
35401.e: There is no fixed number for a petition. Even a single person can submit a petition.
35401.m: A petition does not need a particular number of signatures.

35402.q: Does a petition lead to a popular vote?
35402.e: A petition is a request. It does not lead to a popular vote like an initiative does.
35402.m: A petition does not lead to a popular vote.

35403.q: A class would like a zebra crossing in front of the school. What can it do?
35403.e: With a petition, even a school class can send a wish to the municipality. You do not have to be entitled to vote for this.
35403.m: With a petition, even a school class can express a wish.

35404.q: Where is the right to submit a petition written down?
35404.e: The right of petition is in the Federal Constitution, in Article 33. It is one of the fundamental rights.
35404.m: The right of petition is in the Federal Constitution.

35405.q: What must an authority at least do with a petition?
35405.e: The authority must read the petition and take note of it. But it does not have to carry out the wish.
35405.m: An authority must take note of a petition.

35406.q: May you also address a petition to your own municipality?
35406.e: You can address a petition to many authorities: the municipality, the canton or the Confederation.
35406.m: A petition can go to the municipality, the canton or the Confederation.

35407.q: May someone be punished for signing a petition?
35407.e: The Federal Constitution protects everyone who submits a petition. Nobody may suffer any disadvantage because of it.
35407.m: Anyone who signs a petition must not suffer any disadvantage.

35408.q: Where do you submit the signatures for a federal popular initiative?
35408.e: You submit the signatures for a federal initiative to the Federal Chancellery in Bern.
35408.m: The signatures for an initiative go to the Federal Chancellery.

35409.q: In which city is the Federal Chancellery?
35409.e: The Federal Chancellery is in Bern, where the Federal Council and parliament also work.
35409.m: The Federal Chancellery is in Bern.

35410.q: What does the Federal Chancellery do with the submitted signatures of a popular initiative?
a: It gives them to the Federal Supreme Court
It sends them back to the committee
35410.e: The Federal Chancellery checks and counts the signatures. Then it says whether the initiative has qualified.
35410.m: The Federal Chancellery counts the signatures.

35411.q: Who checks the signature form of a popular initiative before collection begins?
35411.e: Before collection, the Federal Chancellery checks the form and the title. That way the format is right from the start.
35411.m: Before collection, the Federal Chancellery checks the form.

35412.q: Who does the Federal Chancellery mainly work for?
35412.e: The Federal Chancellery is the Federal Council's staff office. It helps the Federal Council with its work.
35412.m: The Federal Chancellery works for the Federal Council.

35413.q: What does the Federal Chancellery check about the title of an initiative?
35413.e: The title of an initiative must not be misleading or contain advertising. Otherwise the Federal Chancellery changes it.
35413.m: The title of an initiative must not be misleading.

35414.q: Which signatures does the Federal Chancellery count in the end?
35414.e: Only valid signatures count. Duplicate or invalid signatures are not counted.
35414.m: The Federal Chancellery only counts valid signatures.

35415.q: Where does the Federal Chancellery announce that an initiative has qualified?
a: In the canton of Bern's official gazette
35415.e: The Federal Gazette is the Confederation's official publication. It states whether an initiative has enough valid signatures.
35415.m: The Federal Chancellery publishes its decisions in the Federal Gazette.

35416.q: What is the group that starts a popular initiative called?
35416.e: A popular initiative is started by an initiative committee. It is responsible for the initiative.
35416.m: An initiative committee starts a popular initiative.

35417.q: What is the minimum number of people in an initiative committee?
35417.e: An initiative committee consists of at least 7 people entitled to vote. These people are responsible for the initiative.
35417.m: An initiative committee has at least 7 members.

a: A group that starts a popular initiative
A commission of the Federal Council
A party in the Council of States
35418.e: The initiative committee is the group of voters who launch a popular initiative. It organises the collection of signatures.
35418.m: An initiative committee starts a popular initiative.

35419.q: Who may take part in an initiative committee?
a: All residents, even without a Swiss passport
Only members of the National Council
Only members of a municipal government
35419.e: The members of the initiative committee must be entitled to vote. That means Swiss citizens aged 18 and over.
35419.m: Only people entitled to vote sit on the initiative committee.
